reader.summary: Israel stood on the brink of a tightly contested general election scheduled for October 27, pitting Prime Minister Netanyahu against former Defense Minister Gadi Eisenkot in a race where no side appeared close to a clean 61-seat mandate. In Gaza, commercial goods had been briefly suspended over a merchant-Hamas tax dispute before Israel announced their return, while the World Food Programme cut its beneficiary count from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, raising winter-shock fears. The West Bank saw a sharp spike in settler violence during the olive harvest, including attacks on European diplomats, a U.S. journalist, and a U.S. congressional candidate; Israel arrested ten suspects. On the diplomatic front, the United States and Israel advanced joint strike planning against Iran, with Secretary Hegseth making an unannounced visit to Jerusalem, while Trump openly endorsed Netanyahu and Vice President Vance withheld his. Large numbers of diaspora Israelis were flying home to vote. The Central Bank held rates steady and raised growth forecasts, but bond markets stayed nervous ahead of the vote. The far right, split between Ben-Gvir, Winter, and other challengers, complicated Netanyahu's coalition arithmetic.

In Gaza, commercial goods will partially resume after the tax-dispute suspension, but the WFP one-third aid cut will fuel visible protests in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem over winter preparedness. West Bank settler violence will intensify, with another round of harvest-season attacks generating arrests and European diplomatic complaints. The U.S.-Israel Iran planning track will stay active but not trigger a full-scale operation, as Washington waits for its November midterms to clear. Markets will track polling shifts more than fundamentals, and the shekel will feel pressure. The week will close with Israel tense, politically unresolved, and much less certain about its direction than it began.
